Revenue is the total amount of money that flows into a person, business, or organization from their normal activities — counted before any expenses or costs are subtracted.

Think of it as the full pile of money you receive. What you do with that pile afterward — paying rent, salaries, bills — doesn't change the revenue figure. Revenue is purely about what came in.
A Simple Example to Ground This

Imagine you run a small lemonade stall. Over the course of a Saturday, you sell 100 cups at ₹10 each. The total money you collect — ₹1,000 — is your revenue.

Now, you spent ₹300 on lemons, sugar, and cups. That ₹300 is your expense. After subtracting it, you're left with ₹700 — that's your profit.

Notice: revenue is the ₹1,000 — the entire amount that came in. Not ₹700. Revenue doesn't care about your costs. It's simply the total money received from doing what you do.

For a business:
A company's revenue comes from selling its products or services. A shoe company earns revenue when customers buy shoes. A software company earns revenue when customers pay for subscriptions. A hotel earns revenue when guests pay for rooms. All of this counts as revenue regardless of how much the company spends to produce or deliver those things.

For a government:
Governments earn revenue primarily through taxes — income tax, sales tax, import duties, and fees. When citizens and businesses pay taxes, that money becomes the government's revenue, which it then uses to fund roads, hospitals, schools, and so on. This is why you'll often hear phrases like "government revenue" or "tax revenue" in news about national budgets.

For an individual (less common but valid):
If you rent out a room in your house for ₹8,000 a month, that ₹8,000 is your rental revenue. If you also do freelance design work and earn ₹15,000 from it, your total revenue from both activities is ₹23,000. Here, revenue simply means all the money you've received.
The Most Important Distinction: Revenue vs. Profit

This is where most learners get confused, so it's worth being very precise.

Revenue = Total money received (before any deductions).
Profit = Money left over after all expenses have been subtracted from revenue.

A company can have enormous revenue and still be losing money — if its expenses are even higher. For example, a startup might earn ₹50 crore in revenue but spend ₹70 crore running the business. Its revenue is ₹50 crore, but it has a loss of ₹20 crore, not a profit.

This is why investors, analysts, and business owners track both revenue and profit separately — revenue tells you how much is coming in; profit tells you whether the business is actually sustainable.
Revenue vs. Income — A Nuance Worth Knowing

In everyday speech, people sometimes use "revenue" and "income" interchangeably, and that's acceptable in casual conversation. But in formal business and accounting language, there's often a distinction:

  • Revenue almost always refers to the top-line total — the gross amount received before anything is taken out.
  • Income (especially "net income") often refers to what remains after expenses have been deducted — essentially, profit.

You'll sometimes hear businesspeople refer to revenue as the "top line" of a financial statement because it appears at the very top, before all the deductions are listed below it. Profit, sitting at the bottom after all subtractions, is called the "bottom line." When someone says "it affects our bottom line," they mean it affects their profit.
Two Kinds of Revenue a Business Can Have

1. Operating revenue — money earned from the company's main activity. For a bakery, this is money from selling bread and cakes. For an airline, it's ticket sales. This is the core, recurring source of revenue that the business was built around.

2. Non-operating revenue — money earned from secondary or incidental activities, not the core business. For example, if that same bakery keeps some money in a savings account and earns interest on it, that interest is non-operating revenue. If a company owns a building and rents out part of it, the rent is non-operating revenue. It's still revenue, but it doesn't come from the company's main purpose.

This distinction matters because operating revenue tells you how healthy the actual business is, while non-operating revenue can be unpredictable or one-time.
How the Word Is Used in Real Life

You'll encounter "revenue" constantly in news, business, and finance. Here are the kinds of sentences where it appears naturally:

  • "The company reported revenue of $5 billion this quarter." — meaning it received $5 billion from its sales activities.
  • "Revenue fell by 12% due to lower consumer demand." — the total money coming in decreased.
  • "The government is looking for new sources of revenue." — ways to bring in more money (new taxes, fees, etc.).
  • "Revenue growth was strong, but the company still posted a loss." — more money came in than before, but expenses were even higher.
  • "Advertising revenue accounts for 80% of the platform's earnings." — most of its incoming money comes from advertisers.
The One-Sentence Definition You Can Always Rely On

Revenue is the total money received by a business, government, or individual from their activities or operations, measured before any expenses or costs are deducted.

Everything else — profit, net income, earnings — comes after you've done something with that revenue. Revenue itself is simply the starting point: the full amount that walked through the door.
